mcqs.q: ‘People with special needs’ refers to individuals who:
opts: Have barriers to good oral health, primarily because of a disability or medical condition
Have no health concerns at all
mcqs.explain: People with special needs are those who have barriers to achieving good oral health primarily because of a disability or medical condition.

mcqs.q: People with special needs include:
opts: The elderly, people with disabilities, and those with complex medical/physical/psychological problems
mcqs.explain: They include the elderly, people who have disabilities, and people with complex medical, physical and psychological problems.

mcqs.q: Compared with the rest of the population, people with special needs have:
opts: More dental disease, more missing teeth, and more difficulty obtaining care
Less dental disease and easier access
mcqs.explain: People with special needs have more dental disease, more missing teeth, and more difficulty obtaining dental care than other segments of the population.

mcqs.q: Providing adequate care for special-care individuals requires a balance between:
opts: Complex medical factors and social factors
mcqs.explain: Adequate care requires a balance between complex medical factors and social factors.

mcqs.q: A common challenge in this group, due to their many medications, is:
mcqs.explain: Xerostomia is a side effect of many medications used by people in this group.

mcqs.q: A reason for pain, suffering and social stigma in special-needs populations is that:
opts: Some caregivers are unaware of the consequences of untreated disease and how to prevent it
mcqs.explain: Some caregivers are not themselves aware of the consequences of untreated dental disease and the procedures to prevent it.

mcqs.q: Because treatment is difficult for people with special needs, the main focus should be on:
mcqs.explain: The difficulty in providing treatment for people with special needs makes the focus on prevention.

mcqs.q: The four obstacles to oral health in people with special needs are:
mcqs.explain: The four obstacles are information obstacles, physical obstacles, behavioral obstacles, and organizational obstacles.

mcqs.q: The key question of the INFORMATION obstacle is:
opts: Do the individual or caregivers understand what needs to be done?
mcqs.explain: Information obstacles ask whether the individual or their caregivers understand what needs to be done.

mcqs.q: The traditional short ‘oral hygiene’ lesson at the end of an appointment:
opts: May have no impact on subsequent behaviour
mcqs.explain: The traditional short ‘oral hygiene’ session at the end of an appointment may not have any impact on subsequent behaviour.

mcqs.q: Effective health-promotion messages are best delivered:
opts: In community settings, partnering with community-based resources
mcqs.explain: It is critical to partner with community-based resources; effective messages are best delivered in community settings (residence, school, work program, etc.).

mcqs.q: In a ‘pyramid’ training program, the dental professional:
opts: Trains a home-health nurse or facility manager who then helps the individuals
Treats every patient personally with no help
mcqs.explain: In a ‘pyramid’ training program, the dental professional trains a home health nurse or residential facility manager on overcoming obstacles.

mcqs.q: ‘Daily mouth care’ messages should:
opts: Use simple language and pictures, deliver small amounts, and test/repeat understanding
Use complex jargon all at once
Be delivered only once with no repetition
mcqs.explain: Messages should use simple language, refer to pictures/diagrams, deliver small amounts at a time, test/repeat understanding, and add new information later.

mcqs.q: To make messages translate to behavior change, you should:
opts: Tailor messages to the values and desires of the person (e.g. motivational interviewing)
Give the same generic message to everyone
mcqs.explain: Tailor messages to the values and desires of the person so they translate to behavior change — for example, motivational interviewing.

mcqs.q: A PHYSICAL barrier in special-care individuals refers to a lack of:
mcqs.explain: Physical barriers mean the individual lacks the musculature, dexterity or coordination to do their oral-care tasks.

mcqs.q: A typical example of a physical barrier is:
opts: Inability to grasp a toothbrush or manipulate dental floss
mcqs.explain: A physical barrier example is simply the inability to grasp a toothbrush or to manipulate dental floss.

mcqs.q: Which adaptation helps overcome a physical barrier to brushing?
opts: A toothbrush with a larger handle (tennis ball or bicycle grip)
mcqs.explain: Toothbrushes can be adapted with a larger handle using a tennis ball or bicycle handle grip; a foam ball can also help pick up the brush.

mcqs.q: ‘Partial participation’ describes a situation where:
opts: The person does as much as they can and the caregiver does the rest
mcqs.explain: Partial participation = the person does as much as they can, and the caregiver does what the person cannot do.

mcqs.q: A technique used to keep the mouth open during partial participation is the:
opts: Tongue-blade mouth prop with proper positioning
Cotton roll under the tongue only
Rubber dam clamp on the lip
mcqs.explain: A technique of partial participation is the tongue-blade mouth prop, used with positioning (e.g. head resting on the caregiver's shoulder).

mcqs.q: In overcoming physical and behavioral obstacles, the dental professional's role is mainly:
mcqs.explain: The role of the dental professional is to educate caregivers — e.g. about behavioral intervention strategies (behavior support).

mcqs.q: The key question of the BEHAVIORAL obstacle is:
opts: Is the individual resistant to preventive procedures?
Do they understand what to do?
mcqs.explain: Behavioral obstacles ask whether the individual is resistant to performing, or having someone else perform, preventive procedures.

mcqs.q: Which is a ‘behavior support’ technique?
opts: Structuring the environment, involving the individual, counseling the caregiver, reinforcers, shaping
mcqs.explain: Behavior support includes structuring the environment, involving the individual, counseling the caregiver, reinforcers/reward systems, and shaping.

mcqs.q: ‘Structuring the environment’ means:
opts: Performing oral hygiene in a setting that makes it seem fun
Removing the individual from their home
mcqs.explain: Structuring the environment might include performing oral hygiene procedures in a setting that makes them seem fun, suited to that individual.

mcqs.q: ‘Involving the individual’ can aid cooperation by:
opts: Increasing choices — e.g. when to brush or the colour of a new toothbrush
Removing all of the individual's choices
mcqs.explain: Involving the individual aids cooperation; increasing choices (e.g. when to brush, or what colour the new toothbrush will be) is an example.

mcqs.q: ‘Counseling the caregiver’ involves:
opts: Counseling the caregiver to pay attention to how the person is doing
Telling the caregiver to ignore the person
mcqs.explain: Counseling the caregiver involves counseling them to pay attention to how the person is doing.

mcqs.q: A ‘reinforcer’ is a method that:
opts: Makes the individual want to continue or increase the activity that produced the reward
mcqs.explain: A reinforcer is a method that results in the individual wanting to continue or increase the activity that produced the reward.

mcqs.q: An example of a SOCIAL reward is:
mcqs.explain: Social rewards include examples like smiling and praise.

mcqs.q: ‘Shaping’ a behaviour means:
opts: Reinforcing an approximation first (reward after 30 s), then requiring more over time
Demanding the full task perfectly on day one
mcqs.explain: Shaping is the reinforcement of an approximation of the task — e.g. a reinforcer after 30 seconds at first, then not until 1–2 minutes later.

mcqs.q: The key question of the ORGANIZATIONAL obstacle is whether there is a system at:
opts: The home, community, or facility that can support the individual and caregivers
mcqs.explain: Organizational obstacles ask whether there is a system in the home, community, or facility that can support them and help overcome the other three obstacles.

mcqs.q: An advantage of having a written PLAN for special-care individuals is that it:
opts: Organizes caregivers' thinking, acts as a communication vehicle, and records progress
Replaces the need for any care
mcqs.explain: A plan helps caregivers organize their thinking, acts as a communication vehicle, and acts as a record of progress.

saqs.q: Define ‘people with special needs’ and state three things they experience more than others.
saqs.a: People with special needs = individuals who have barriers to achieving good oral health primarily because of a disability or medical condition (elderly, disabled, medically/physically/psychologically complex). They have more dental disease, more missing teeth, and more difficulty obtaining dental care.

saqs.q: List the four obstacles to oral health in people with special needs.
How can information obstacles be overcome?
saqs.a: Deliver health-promotion messages in community settings (not just a short chairside lesson), partner with community-based resources, use ‘pyramid’ training (train a nurse/facility manager), and make daily mouth-care messages simple (pictures, small amounts, test/repeat). Tailor messages to the person's values (e.g. motivational interviewing).

saqs.q: What is ‘partial participation’, and give an aid for physical obstacles.
saqs.a: Partial participation = the person does as much as they can and the caregiver does the rest (e.g. using a tongue-blade mouth prop with good positioning). Physical aids include a toothbrush with a larger handle (tennis ball / bicycle grip) or a foam ball to help grasp the brush.

saqs.q: List the behavior-support techniques for behavioral obstacles.
saqs.a: 1) Structuring the environment (make it fun), 2) Involving the individual (offer choices), 3) Counseling the caregiver, 4) Reinforcers / reward systems (incl. social rewards — smiling, praise), 5) Shaping (reinforce an approximation first).

saqs.q: Why is it important to ‘put it all together’ in a plan, and what are its advantages?
saqs.a: A plan applies the various techniques, is communicated among the people involved, and must be understood by caregivers. Advantages: it helps caregivers organize their thinking, acts as a communication vehicle, and serves as a record of progress.
